analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering medical, dental, and hospital care, funded by a new 5% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The bill, one of the first introduced in the 110th Congress with no cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national health insurance program run through a new National Health Insurance Board in the Department of Health and Human Services, with doctors, dentists, hospitals, and other providers paid from a dedicated fund for serving eligible people. Benefits would have included medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services such as expensive drugs and eyeglasses, and patients would have had free choice of provider. The money would have come from a new 5% federal value-added tax — a national sales tax collected at each stage of production — on most goods and services, with food, housing, medical care, exports, and government purchases exempted. Medicare beneficiaries would have been limited to services Medicare does not cover. The bill never left the two House committees it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have covered eligible individuals — broadly, workers and Social Security beneficiaries meeting wage-history thresholds and their dependents, with states able to buy coverage for the needy using existing federal grants — for doctor visits, dental and podiatric care, home nursing, up to 60 days of hospital care, and auxiliary services like X-rays, expensive prescriptions, and eyeglasses. Patients would have chosen their own doctors and hospitals. Medicare beneficiaries would have gained coverage for the services Medicare does not pay for.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have made medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services (including expensive prescribed drugs and eyeglasses) available as benefits to eligible individuals in every health-service area of the country.

Every covered person would have had full freedom to choose and change their physician, dentist, and hospital, and providers would have been paid through fee schedules, per-capita payments, or salaries.
The program would have been financed by a new 5% value-added tax on most commercial sales, with all of that revenue dedicated to a National Health Care Trust Fund that pays the benefits.

Funds would have been allotted to the states on the basis of population, available professional services and facilities, and compensation costs, with the express aim of improving services where personnel and facilities are below the national average.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and businesses would have paid a new 5% federal value-added tax on most purchases of goods and services, collected at each stage of production. Food, housing, medical care, exports, interest, government entities, and some tax-exempt organizations would have been exempt. Providers who joined the program would have accepted fee schedules, per-capita payments, or salaries set with regard to regional conditions, and hospitals would have been paid on the basis of reasonable costs subject to Board-set maximum rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed a new 5% federal value-added tax on most sales of goods and services, a broad levy that reaches ordinary consumers' purchases even though food, housing, and medical care were exempted.

The bill contained no binding cost-control mechanism; it only required the Secretary of HHS to study methods of controlling the costs of providing benefits, so spending could have grown beyond the 5% tax's yield.

The bill allowed the National Health Insurance Board to limit dental, home-nursing, or auxiliary services for a period if personnel, facilities, or funds were inadequate, meaning some promised benefits could have been rationed or delayed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been very large: everyone would be covered for doctor, dental, and hospital care with free choice of provider, paid for by a broad 5% value-added tax. The costs were also real: a new federal tax on most purchases, an enormous new federal health program with no proven price controls — the bill merely required a study of cost-control methods — and a health-services section that could have limited some benefits if providers or money ran short. Whether a VAT would have been more or less burdensome than the premiums, deductibles, and administrative overhead it replaced was never tested in this or any other chamber, because the bill was never even discussed in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Dingell on January 4, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On February 2, 2007 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no hearings, markup, or floor vote followed during the 110th Congress.
The bill drew zero cosponsors, so no other member signed on to push it forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo, including private health insurers and everyone who would have paid the new tax or borne the transition, was left untouched. Working families with unmet medical needs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; private insurers kept their role

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell (D-MI)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the opening day of the 110th Congress, laying out a national health insurance program financed by a 5% value-added tax.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it referred the bill's health provisions to its Subcommittee on Health on February 2, 2007, where the bill sat without further action.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral, with jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no recorded action on it, including on its value-added tax title.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Private health insurers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed national health insurance proposals of this era as a threat to their business; the bill's absence of cosponsors and its quiet death in committee are consistent with the well-documented hostility such proposals faced, though no industry action on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split over the bill ever took shape on the floor or in a vote.

industries.note: A national health insurance program paying providers directly would have displaced the private role in covering basic care for the eligible population. Private insurers had no guaranteed channel in the bill. Public health insurance proposals of this kind died in this era without the industry being forced to compete with them.

Hospitals would have been paid for treating the whole eligible population, but on 'reasonable cost' bases with Board-set maximum rates and payment based on the least expensive multiple-bed accommodation. Guaranteed volume, capped rates.

Practitioners who joined would have gained a large paying patient population with payments sized to professional income, but subject to Board-established specialist standards and fee, per-capita, or salary payment methods. Participation was voluntary; no practitioner was compelled to join.

industries.industry: Employers and workers who currently pay private premiums
industries.note: Replacing premiums and out-of-pocket costs with a 5% value-added tax would have shifted who pays for health care: away from premiums tied to employment and toward a broad consumption tax. Whether any given household paid more or less would depend on its income and spending.
